Adult female mountain chickens attain a remarkably large body size for a leptodactylid frog, with the largest individuals reaching a snout-vent length of 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters]. In contrast, adult males are notably smaller, achieving a maximum snout-vent length of only 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is among the most extreme documented within the genus Leptodactylus and is likely driven by intense female-female competition for nesting sites in the species’ foam nests. Newly hatched larvae emerge from the egg mass at a surprisingly advanced developmental stage; the wet weight of a neonate is approximately 0.0141 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0141 grams], a value derived directly from the diameter of the yolk-laden egg, which measures about 3 millimeters. The tadpoles are endotrophic and develop entirely within the foam nest, feeding on unfertilized trophic eggs deposited by the attending female.

The unfertilized trophic eggs that sustain the developing larvae are produced at a remarkable rate under controlled thermal conditions. At a constant ambient temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a single gravid female can generate and deposit approximately 25,000 trophic eggs per year [Ri = approximately 25,000 trophic eggs per year] as part of her maximum reproductive output. This extraordinarily high provisioning rate is essential for supporting the entirely lecithotrophic larval phase, during which the tadpoles do not capture any external prey. The female’s investment in trophic ova is thus a direct analogue to yolk provisioning in oviparous species, but it is extended temporally across the entire period of larval development within the nest. The total number of trophic eggs produced over the course of a single reproductive bout can exceed several thousand, reflecting a massive maternal energetic expenditure that is unmatched among Caribbean anurans of comparable body size.

The complete larval period is relatively brief for such a large-bodied anuran, with metamorphosis occurring after approximately 45 days  when the larvae are reared at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. At the metamorphic climax, the newly transformed froglet possesses a snout-vent length of roughly 1.98 centimeters . This measurement is derived from a total length of about 11 centimeters, of which the tail accounts for between 79 and 84 percent of the overall body length prior to resorption. The transition from a fully aquatic, gill-breathing tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile requires substantial morphological reorganisation, including the complete resorption of the tail fin and the keratinisation of the skin. Juveniles emerging from the nest are therefore capable of immediate terrestrial locomotion and begin foraging for small invertebrates within days of completing metamorphosis, though they remain vulnerable to desiccation until they reach a more robust body size.

Sexual maturity in the mountain chicken is not reached until several years after the larval-juvenile transition. Under the same thermal regime (27 °C [T = 27 °C]), females typically experience their first successful reproductive event at approximately 3 years after metamorphosis [tR = approximately 3 years after metamorphosis]. This delayed onset of breeding is consistent with the species’ relatively slow life-history pace, which also includes an impressive maximum lifespan. Captive individuals have been documented to survive for up to 12 years [am = up to 12 years] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a longevity that is exceptional among Caribbean anurans and likely reflects the species’ large body size and reduced predation pressure on Dominica and Montserrat, its two remaining island strongholds. The extended interval between metamorphosis and first reproduction allows ample time for somatic growth, as females must achieve a substantial body size before they can bear the energetic burden of producing both fertilized and trophic ova. Mature females can reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2,060 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,060 grams], making them one of the heaviest frog species in the world.

The maximum recorded body mass for an adult female, approximately 2,060 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,060 grams], places the mountain chicken among the largest living anurans, comparable in mass to the African goliath frog. This impressive mass is attained through a prolonged growth phase that continues well after the achievement of sexual maturity. Field surveys on Dominica have documented gravid females weighing over two kilograms, a mass that reflects the accumulation of both somatic tissue and a massive complement of ovarian follicles. The species’ very low fecundity per reproductive event—only a few dozen fertilized eggs per clutch—is offset by the production of thousands of trophic ova, which together constitute the bulk of the female’s reproductive investment. At the same 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the oldest known wild individual was estimated to be 12 years [am = 12 years] of age based on mark-recapture data, confirming that this species exhibits one of the longest lifespans documented for any West Indian amphibian.
